736.title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
736.hook: a shepherd boy with a sling and no armor faces a giant
736.howItsDone: Jews read David and Goliath as part of the Former Prophets, and many readers take it as a story of courage and of trust in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shepherd with a harp, and a king whose dark lifted. Your line was music lifts. Did you send someone a song? Today, the same shepherd, with a very different tool in his hand. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

Two armies on two mountains, a valley between them. Every morning and every evening a Philistine champion named Goliath walks out into that valley in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam, and shouts the same challenge: choose a man, and let him come down to me. And Saul and all Israel, the text says, are dismayed and greatly afraid. Into this walks the youngest son of Jesse, carrying food. David's father has sent him to bring bread to his older brothers at the front and see how they're doing. He hears the challenge. And he asks a question of his own: who is this, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE VALLEY.` → `CHOOSE A MAN, AND LET HIM COME.` → `A BOY BRINGING BREAD.`

segments.voice: His oldest brother, Eliab, is furious: why did you come down here? I know your pride. But word reaches Saul, and David is brought to the king. Your servant will go and fight him, he says. Saul says: you're a boy, and he's been a man of war since his youth. And David answers with his own experience. When a lion or a bear took a lamb from the flock, I went after it and took the lamb from its mouth. The LORD who saved me from the lion and the bear will save me from this Philistine. So Saul dresses David in his own armor: a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, a sword. And David tries to walk, and can't. I can't go in these, he says, I haven't tried them. And he takes them off. This is the heart of the story. He doesn't go out in the king's equipment, pretending to be a soldier. He goes out as what he is. He takes his staff, and "chose him five smooth stones out of the brook," and puts them in his shepherd's bag, with his sling in his hand. Goliath sees him and mocks him. David answers: you come to me with a sword and a spear, "but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts." And then, the battle is the LORD's. He runs toward the Philistine, takes one stone, slings it, and it sinks into Goliath's forehead, and he falls on his face. One stone. The text even notes that there was no sword in David's hand. He picked five, and needed one. He faced the giant in the valley with the small tools he actually knew how to use.
screen: `THE LION, THE BEAR, THE LAMB.` · `SAUL'S ARMOR DOESN'T FIT.` · `IN THE NAME OF THE LORD OF HOSTS.` · `HE PICKED FIVE, AND NEEDED ONE.` · then, large: `FIVE SMOOTH STONES OUT OF THE BROOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face one big thing with small tools. Settle, and breathe. Name the giant in your valley right now. A debt, a diagnosis, a hard conversation, a project you can't start. Notice whether you've been trying to fight it in someone else's armor, someone else's method, someone else's idea of how it should be done. Then ask: what are my smooth stones? What do I already know how to do? Make a call. Write one paragraph. Ask for help. Take one walk. Choose one small stone and decide when you'll throw it. If you pray, you can bring the giant to God as David did. The bell holds the time.
Five smooth stones. What David chose from the brook when he set aside Saul's armor and went out to face Goliath with a sling. He picked five; one was enough. Today's word.
Your line: five smooth stones. Today, throw your one small stone at the big thing: the call, the paragraph, the first step, with the tools you actually have. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: As his own soul (1 Samuel 18:1–4)
737.hook: Jonathan loves David as his own soul and gives him his robe
737.howItsDone: Jews read the friendship of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the teaching in Pirkei Avot about love that depends on nothing is studied with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shepherd with a sling and no armor walked out to meet a giant. Your line was five smooth stones. What big thing did you face with small tools? Today, someone standing near the king was watching him. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

The fight is over. David stands in front of King Saul, and Saul asks him a plain question: whose son are you? David answers, the son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem. That's all he says, as far as the text tells us. But someone else is in the room. Jonathan, the king's son. A fighter himself, the one who once climbed a rocky pass with only his armor-bearer beside him to face a Philistine camp. Later in the book, Saul will tell him outright that as long as David lives, Jonathan's own kingdom won't be secure. Jonathan has every reason to see this shepherd as a rival. And when David has finished speaking, the text turns away from the king and looks at his son.
screen: `WHOSE SON ARE YOU?` → `JONATHAN IS LISTENING.` → `THE KING'S SON, AND A RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening of chapter eighteen. The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, "and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." The Hebrew word under soul is nefesh, and it's wider than the English. It can mean life, breath, the self that's alive in you. So Jonathan loves David the way a person holds on to their own life. And the phrase doesn't come once. Two verses later, Jonathan makes a covenant with David, a binding promise, and the reason given is the same: because he loved him as his own soul. Then he does something with his hands. He strips off the robe he's wearing and gives it to David. Then his garments. Then his sword, his bow, his belt. Everything a prince and a soldier would wear into a room, he hands to a shepherd. The text doesn't explain the gesture. Some readers hear the heir to the throne quietly handing over what marks him as heir. Others hear something simpler: a friend dressing his friend in the best he has. Either way, nothing comes back the other direction. David gives nothing in these verses. The rabbis noticed this friendship. In Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, there's a teaching about love. Love that depends on some thing ends when the thing is gone. Love that doesn't depend on anything never ends. And the example they give of the second kind is the love of David and Jonathan: a friendship that isn't about what the other person can do for you.
screen: `KNIT, SOUL TO SOUL.` · `NEFESH: LIFE, BREATH, SELF.` · `THE ROBE, THE SWORD, THE BOW.` · then, large: `AS HIS OWN SOUL.` · then: `LOVE THAT DEPENDS ON NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a friend something of yours. Settle, and breathe. Let one friend come to mind, someone whose life you'd hold close. Then look around your own life for something to hand them. Not something you were throwing out. A book you love. A jacket. An hour. A thing you made. A skill you could teach. Choose one, and picture putting it in their hands. Notice whether part of you wants to hold it back, and let that be there too. If you pray, you can hold the verse: he loved him as his own soul. The bell holds the time.
As his own soul. Nefesh, the self that breathes, and Jonathan loving David that way, with a covenant and a robe. Today's word.
Your line: as his own soul. Today, give that one thing away, and don't ask for anything back. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: two young men become good friends.
what it means: the king's son loves a possible rival as his own life, binds himself to him, and gives him his robe and weapons.
what a scholar hears: Pirkei Avot holds up David and Jonathan as its example of love that depends on nothing, and so never ends.

738.title: Through the window (1 Samuel 19:11–17)
738.hook: Michal lets David down through a window to escape her father
738.howItsDone: Jews read Michal's rescue of David in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; Psalm 59, whose heading ties it to this night, is read in the book of Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king's son gave a shepherd his robe, his sword and his bow. Your line was as his own soul. What did you put in a friend's hands? Today, the king's daughter saves the same man's life. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

Night, and there are men outside the house. King Saul has sent them to watch David's door and kill him in the morning. Inside is David, and his wife, Michal, who is Saul's own daughter. A chapter earlier, the text says plainly that Michal loved David. Now she knows something he may not. She tells him: if you don't save your life tonight, tomorrow you'll be killed. There's no time for a plan with many parts. The front door is watched. She has a house, a husband, a father who is the king, and maybe a few hours. What she does next happens at a window.
screen: `MEN WATCH THE DOOR.` → `SAUL'S DAUGHTER, DAVID'S WIFE.` → `TONIGHT, OR NOT AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The verse is short and fast: "So Michal let David down through the window; and he went, and fled, and escaped." Three verbs for David, one after another, like footsteps. Then Michal turns back into the room and starts buying him time. She takes the household image the text calls teraphim, lays it in the bed, puts a pillow of goats' hair where his head would be, and covers it with a cloth. When Saul's messengers come, she says David is sick. Saul sends them back: bring him to me in the bed, so I can kill him. They pull back the cover and find the image and a goat's-hair pillow. Notice who stands in the danger now. David is gone. Michal is the one facing her father. Saul asks why she deceived him and let his enemy escape. And she answers with a story: David said to her, let me go, why should I kill you? It may not be true. The text doesn't say. It reads like a daughter shielding herself from a father who, by this point in the book, has already thrown a spear at David. So the window works two ways. It's how David gets out, and it's where Michal stays behind. She can't climb down after him. Her rescue costs her something, and the story lets her pay it alone. There's a small echo here, too. The heading of Psalm fifty-nine ties that psalm to this very night, when Saul sent men to watch the house to kill him. A prayer, by tradition, from inside the danger she helped him out of.
screen: `LET DOWN THROUGH THE WINDOW.` · `AN IMAGE IN THE BED.` · `MICHAL FACES HER FATHER.` · then, large: `HE WENT, AND FLED, AND ESCAPED.` · then: `PSALM 59: THAT SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone out of danger. Danger doesn't always look like men at the door. It's a friend in a bad stretch, a coworker getting blamed, a kid being picked on, someone you know who's in over their head. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind. Then look for the window: the one small opening you could give them. A call. A word to the right person. A place to stay. A ride. Choose it, and hold it until the bell. If you pray, you can hold that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Through the window. Michal lowers David out, and stays behind to face her father with an image in the bed. Today's word.
Your line: through the window. Today, open the window you found for someone, before the morning comes. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

739.title: The arrows (1 Samuel 20)
739.hook: Jonathan signals with arrows, and the friends part in tears
739.howItsDone: Jews read the parting of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the chapter's feast of the new moon, Rosh Chodesh, is still marked in the Jewish calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Michal lowered David through the window and stayed behind to face her father. Your line was through the window. Did you find an opening for someone? Today, a signal in a field. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

A code, worked out in advance between two friends, because they can't risk being seen talking. David will hide in a field, beside a stone. Jonathan will come out as if for target practice, with a boy to fetch his arrows. He'll shoot three arrows to the side. Then he'll call out to the boy. If he shouts that the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe. Come home. If he shouts that the arrows are beyond you, the king means to kill him. Go. Jonathan has to find out which it is at his father's table, at the feast of the new moon. And then he has to say it out loud, in front of a boy who has no idea what the words mean.
screen: `DAVID HIDES BY THE STONE.` → `THREE ARROWS AND A BOY.` → `THIS SIDE, OR BEYOND?`

segments.voice: At the feast, David's seat is empty. On the second day Saul asks about it, and Jonathan covers for his friend. Saul explodes. He shames his own son, tells him that as long as David lives, Jonathan's kingdom won't stand, and throws a spear at him. Now Jonathan knows. In the morning he goes out to the field. The boy runs, Jonathan shoots past him, and he calls out the line the two friends agreed on. The plan was, "Behold, the arrows are beyond thee." The answer is go. Then Jonathan adds more, as if to a slow servant: make speed, hurry, don't stay. The words are for the boy, and for the man behind the stone. And here the plan breaks down, in the best way. The code was built so they wouldn't have to meet. Jonathan sends the boy back to town with his weapons. David comes out from his hiding place and bows to the ground. They kiss each other and weep together, and the text says David wept the more. Jonathan's last words are a blessing and a promise. Go in peace. We've sworn in the name of the Lord, he says, that the Lord will be between me and you, and between my children and your children, for ever. Notice how he says goodbye. Not by pretending it's fine. Not by leaving on a signal. He sends the witness away, and they say it face to face. The arrows told David everything he needed to know. The goodbye told him something the arrows couldn't.
screen: `THE EMPTY SEAT. THE SPEAR.` · `A SHOUT TO THE BOY.` · `THE CODE BREAKS: THEY MEET.` · then, large: `THE ARROWS ARE BEYOND THEE.` · then: `GO IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one goodbye properly. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who's leaving, or who you're leaving. A coworker moving on. A friend moving away. A kid going off. Someone at the end of their life. A goodbye that keeps getting done by text, or by a wave, or not at all. Think what you'd want to say face to face, the way Jonathan sent the boy away so he could say it. One sentence is enough. Hold it. If you pray, you can hold Jonathan's words: go in peace. The bell holds the time.
The arrows. A signal shot past a boy in a field, that told David to go, and a goodbye said in person anyway. Today's word.
Your line: the arrows are beyond thee. Today, say the goodbye you've been putting off, and say it to their face if you can. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

740.title: Sparing Saul (1 Samuel 24)
740.hook: David cuts Saul's robe in the cave but will not harm him
740.carry: I will not put forth my hand
740.howItsDone: Jews read David sparing Saul in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and some teachers read it alongside the Torah's warnings against taking revenge or bearing a grudge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arrows past a boy in a field, and two friends weeping goodbye. Your line was the arrows are beyond thee. Did you say a goodbye properly? Today, David is on the run, and the king walks into his hiding place. Day seven hundred forty.

A cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, wild-goat country. Deep inside, in the dark, David and his men are hiding from the king who wants him dead. And then the king himself walks in, alone, to relieve himself. He has no idea who's at the back of the cave. David's men lean in and whisper. This is the day, they say. The day God promised: your enemy, delivered into your hand. Do to him whatever seems good to you. The man who hunted David is a few steps away, alone, with his back to the dark. David gets up, and creeps forward in the dark.
screen: `A CAVE AT EN-GEDI.` → `THE KING WALKS IN ALONE.` → `THIS IS THE DAY, THEY SAY.`

segments.voice: David reaches Saul and quietly cuts off the corner of his robe. That's all. And then, the text says, David's heart struck him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt. He hasn't harmed Saul at all. All he has done is cut a piece of cloth. Robes matter in this book. Earlier, when Saul grabbed the prophet Samuel's robe and it tore, Samuel told him the kingdom had been torn from him the same way. So a torn corner of the king's robe is not a small thing. David turns to his men and says, in effect, God forbid. I will not put forth my hand against my lord, because he is the Lord's anointed. He holds his men back, and Saul walks out of the cave unharmed. Then David does something risky. He follows Saul out, calls after him, bows to the ground, and holds up the corner of the robe. Look, he says. I was close enough to cut this, and I didn't kill you. Let the Lord judge between us, but my hand won't be on you. And Saul, the hunter, weeps out loud. Is this your voice, my son David? He says David is more righteous than he is, because David repaid him good for evil. Here's what makes this hard. David's men are using religious language: this is the day God promised. David answers with religious language too, the Lord's anointed. Same God, opposite conclusions. The text sides with the one who keeps his hand still. And it notices that even the small cut hurt his conscience.
screen: `A CORNER OF THE ROBE.` · `HIS HEART STRUCK HIM.` · `THE LORD'S ANOINTED.` · then, large: `I WILL NOT PUT FORTH MY HAND.` · then: `IS THIS YOUR VOICE, MY SON?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: spare someone you could hurt. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who's wronged you, or who's simply in your power right now: a person whose secret you know, whose mistake you could repeat, whose weak spot you could press. Notice the voices that say this is the day. You'd be in the right. Then notice your hand. Picture it staying still. You don't have to forgive them in the next two minutes. Just choose not to cut. If you pray, you can hold David's words: I will not put forth my hand. The bell holds the time.
Sparing Saul. A king in the dark, a corner of his robe, and a hand that stays still. Today's word.
Your line: I will not put forth my hand. Today, when you get the chance to land a blow on someone, in words or otherwise, don't take it. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: Abigail (1 Samuel 25)
741.hook: a wise woman stops David's rage with food and words
741.howItsDone: Jews read Abigail's story in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the Talmud remembers her among the women it counts as prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cave, a king alone, and a corner of his robe. Your line was I will not put forth my hand. Did you hold back a blow? Today, David nearly doesn't, and someone stops him. Day seven hundred forty-one.
screen: `I WILL NOT PUT FORTH MY HAND.`

segments.voice: "Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse?" That's the answer David's young men bring back. They had gone, politely, to a rich sheep owner named Nabal at shearing time, a time of feasting. David's band had been camped near Nabal's shepherds out in the wilderness and had kept them safe. Now they were asking for whatever he could spare. Nabal sends them off with an insult. David hears it and says one thing to his men: gird on your swords. He buckles on his own. By the time a servant runs to tell Nabal's wife what's happening, David is already on the road, and he's not coming to talk.
screen: `SHEARING TIME AT CARMEL.` → `WHO IS DAVID?` → `GIRD ON YOUR SWORDS.`

segments.voice: The servant tells Abigail everything. The text calls her a woman of good understanding, and it calls her husband churlish. She doesn't wait. She doesn't tell Nabal. She loads donkeys with bread and wine, meat and grain, raisins and figs, and rides out. She meets David coming down a mountain path. He has already sworn that by morning not one male of Nabal's house will be left. Abigail gets off her donkey, falls at his feet, and says, upon me, my lord, let the blame be. Then she talks, and each step of her speech counts. She doesn't defend her husband; she says his name means fool, and folly is with him. She takes the fault onto herself. Then she looks past today. When God has made you ruler over Israel, she says, you won't want this on your heart: that you shed blood for nothing, that you saved yourself with your own hand. She gives an angry man a picture of the person he'll want to have been. And David stops. Blessed be the Lord who sent you to meet me today, he says, "and blessed be thy discretion," and blessed be you, who kept me from bloodguilt. The Hebrew word for discretion is ta'am, which also means taste. Good judgment, the sense to tell what fits the moment. Notice who got David from rage to blessing. Not a soldier. Not one of his own men. A woman with food and the right words at the right moment. The rabbis of the Talmud remembered her: they list Abigail among the women of Israel they count as prophets.
screen: `SHE DOESN'T WAIT.` · `UPON ME BE THE BLAME.` · `PICTURE WHO YOU'LL WANT TO BE.` · then, large: `BLESSED BE THY DISCRETION.` · then: `TA'AM: TASTE, JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: calm someone's anger. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who is angry right now, or often is. A partner, a parent, a friend with a grievance, a customer. Abigail did three things: she came with something in her hands, she took some of the weight on herself, and she pointed past the anger to who he'd want to be. Pick one of those for your person. What could you bring? What could you own? What could you help them remember about themselves? Hold one answer. The bell holds the time.
Abigail. The woman of good understanding who rode out with bread and wine, met David's rage on a mountain path, and turned it. Today's word.
Your line: blessed be thy discretion. Today, when someone near you is heating up, bring something, own something, and say one thing about who they really are. Day seven hundred forty-one.

options: warn your husband and let him handle it.

what a scholar hears: her discretion is ta'am, taste; and the Talmud lists Abigail among the women it counts as prophets.

742.title: The woman of Endor (1 Samuel 28)
742.hook: desperate Saul consults a medium, who then insists on feeding him
742.tomorrow: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1:17–27)
742.howItsDone: Jews read Saul's night at Endor in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; the Torah forbids consulting mediums and the dead, and commentators have debated what happened in the woman's house.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abigail rode out with bread and wine and talked David down from bloodshed. Your line was blessed be thy discretion. Did you cool someone's anger? Today, another woman, another meal, and a king at the end of his rope. Day seven hundred forty-two.

Samuel is dead and buried. The Philistine army is camped across the valley, and when Saul sees it, the text says, his heart trembles greatly. He asks God what to do, and nothing comes. No dream. No answer by the Urim, the priest's lots. No prophet. Silence from every direction. So the king does the thing he himself had outlawed. Saul had driven the mediums and the ghost-raisers out of the land. Now he tells his servants: find me a woman who can call up the dead. They know of one, at Endor. Saul takes off his royal clothes, puts on other clothes, and goes by night.
screen: `SAMUEL IS DEAD.` → `NO DREAM, NO URIM, NO PROPHET.` → `BY NIGHT, TO ENDOR.`

segments.voice: The woman is wary. You know what Saul did to people like me, she says. Are you setting a trap? The disguised king swears by the Lord she won't be punished. He asks for Samuel. And when she sees what comes up, she screams, because now she knows who her visitor is. She describes an old man coming up, wrapped in a robe. Readers have argued over what really happened in that room, and the text doesn't settle it. What it does give us is Samuel's message, and it is crushing. The kingdom has been torn from you. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. Saul falls full length on the ground. There's no strength left in him; he hasn't eaten all day or all night. Here the story turns, and this is the part to carry. The woman goes to him. She says, I took my life in my hand and listened to you. Now you listen to me. Let me set a bit of bread before you, and eat, so you'll have strength for the road. He refuses. I won't eat. His servants join in, and she keeps pressing, until he gets up off the floor and sits on the bed. Then she moves fast. She has a fatted calf in the house. She kills it, takes flour, kneads it, bakes flat bread. She sets it before Saul and his servants, and they eat, and they get up and go out into the night. The Torah forbids what she does for a living. And the text still lets her be the one who shows Saul kindness that night. She fed him.
screen: `ARE YOU SETTING A TRAP?` · `AN OLD MAN IN A ROBE.` · `SAUL FALLS. NO STRENGTH LEFT.` · then, large: `SHE FED HIM.` · then: `THE CALF, THE BREAD, THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone in despair. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who's on the floor right now, in whatever way: grieving, exhausted, scared, out of options. Despair can forget the body. Saul had stopped eating. The woman of Endor didn't argue with Saul's fear or fix his future. She put bread in front of him. Think what the bread would be for your person. A meal dropped at the door. Coffee. Sitting with them while they eat. Choose it. If you pray, you can hold their name in your mind. The bell holds the time.
The woman of Endor. A medium the king had outlawed, who saw him fall and wouldn't let him leave hungry. Today's word.

Your line: she fed him. Today, bring food to someone who's low. And look back at this week: five smooth stones, as his own soul, through the window, the arrows, sparing Saul, Abigail, and the woman of Endor. Day seven hundred forty-two.
